propositions.text: Claimants are Afghan citizens seeking protection under Sections 96 and 97 of IRPA.
Claimants allege protection under Sections 96 and 97 of IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states claimants are Afghan citizens seeking protection under Sections 96 and 97 of IRPA, as alleged by the applicant.

propositions.text: Claimant is from Kabul and was a XXXX; husband worked on XXXX projects.
Husband received threatening calls from Taliban Commander XXXX to leave jobs with puppet government in 2011.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant states claimant is from Kabul, was a XXXX, and husband received Taliban threats in 2011 to leave jobs.

propositions.text: In 2011, husband spoke to smuggler about coming to Canada; in 2012 he went to brothers for money but never returned.
Claimant believes husband was taken by Taliban Commander XXXX; police advised reporting to another province but claimant did not due to planned departure.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant states husband planned to come to Canada, disappeared in 2012, believed taken by Taliban; police advised reporting but claimant did not.

propositions.text: Claimants are not Convention refugees under Section 96 as no well-founded fear of persecution on Convention grounds.
Claimants are not persons in need of protection under Section 97 as removal would not subject them to risk to life or cruel treatment.
Panel's reasons for findings follow.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under Sections 96 and 97, and will explain reasons.

propositions.text: Claimant gave majority of oral testimony; counsel questioned minor claimant at hearing end.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes claimant gave most oral testimony; minor was questioned by counsel at hearing end.

propositions.text: Panel considered identity, credibility, well-foundedness of fear, risk to life, and all evidence and submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it considered identity, credibility, well-foundedness, risk, evidence, and submissions.

propositions.text: Claimants are Afghan citizens per passports, but claimant failed to establish husband is minor's father.
Husband's name missing on claimant's passport and taskera; minor's taskera lists husband’s name.
Panel doubts claimant was married to alleged husband and doubts mother-son relationship due to lack of documents and name dissimilarity.
Claimant gave inconsistent age at birth; panel finds claimants are not mother and son.
No post-hearing request for documents was made by claimant or counsel.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants are Afghan citizens but doubts marriage and mother-son relationship due to missing documents and inconsistencies.

propositions.text: Claimant could not document route to Canada or presence in Afghanistan after 2011; arrival date in Canada unknown.
Possible claimants were outside Afghanistan after 2011; full analysis of prior claims or delays is limited.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant failed to document route or presence in Afghanistan after 2011, limiting full analysis of claim timing.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges she was a XXXX in Afghanistan, supported by Exhibit C-7.
Exhibit C-7 was allegedly issued in Afghani language but presented in English without notation; claimant admitted tampering.
Panel finds document not genuine and draws negative inference on claimant's credibility.
Document given no weight; claimant not found to be a XXXX as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges claimant was a XXXX; court finds document tampered, not genuine, and claimant not a XXXX, harming credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges husband was a laborer per PIF and Exhibit R/A-2.
Exhibit C-11 job letter indicates husband was a XXXX XXXX XXXX, different from laborer.
Claimant's explanation of inconsistent occupations is unconvincing; negative inference on credibility made.
Job letter given little weight; claimant not employed as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges husband was laborer; court finds inconsistent evidence and negative credibility inference, rejecting employment claim.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges Taliban Commander XXXX threatened her, causing her to leave Afghanistan.
No evidence that commander exists or had alleged role; night letters not signed or mentioning him.
No police report of night letters; claimant omitted letters from PIF, negative credibility inference made.
Claimant's testimony about husband's police report contradicts earlier narrative; no police report exists.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges Taliban threats; court finds no evidence, omissions, and contradictions, negatively affecting credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant testified about three threat calls threatening to kill minor if jobs not quit.
Claimant omitted threats to kill herself and husband from testimony; explanation rejected; negative credibility inference made.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges threat calls; court finds omissions and rejects explanations, negatively impacting credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant presented night letter about not sending girls to school, though she has no daughters.
Claimant said letter was not addressed to her but to mothers she knows sending children to school.
Panel rejects explanation as claimant not a XXXX; finds night letters not genuine and threat calls did not occur.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant presents night letters; court rejects explanations, finds letters not genuine and threat calls did not occur.

propositions.text: Claimant testified quitting job as XXXX in 2011 due to threats, but gave inconsistent dates.
Claimant's explanations for date inconsistencies rejected; negative credibility inferences made.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges quitting job due to threats; court rejects inconsistent date explanations, negatively affecting credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges husband was kidnapped and reported to Kabul police, who referred her elsewhere; no report made.
No police or media reports document alleged kidnapping; claimant's claim unsupported.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges husband's kidnapping; court finds no supporting reports, rejecting claim.

propositions.text: Due to credibility concerns, claimant's evidence is overall not credible and insufficient for refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's evidence overall not credible and insufficient to support refugee protection claim.

propositions.text: Minor testified father kidnapped and mother at risk for being a XXXX, so he is at risk.
Panel rejects minor's argument as related allegations were rejected above.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant's minor alleges risk; court rejects argument as related allegations were rejected.

propositions.text: Minor fears abduction and recruitment by Taliban as a 16-year-old from Taliban stronghold and same ethnicity.
Minor first said he was 17, raising identity concerns; explanation rejected; doubts on minor's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant's minor fears Taliban recruitment; court doubts minor's credibility due to inconsistent age statement.

propositions.text: Claimant added fear of forced recruitment for minor only at hearing end without prior mention; negative credibility inference made.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's late addition of minor's forced recruitment fear an embellishment, negatively affecting credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant is female and may face risk in Afghanistan without male protection, but panel doubts claimant would be without husband if returned.
Panel finds claimant would not be subject to persecution for being female without husband due to credibility concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant female and possibly at risk, but doubts she would be without husband if returned, so no persecution found.

propositions.text: The Panel considered the situation of women in Afghanistan generally.
Whether the Taliban could target any females in Afghanistan for kidnapping or dress code violations.
No allegation or convincing evidence that such targeting happened in the past or worsened since 2011 when claimants left.
No persuasive evidence that the female claimant is more likely a Taliban target than other Afghan females.
No allegation that the family is high profile to attract Taliban attention; prior allegations about claimant and husband were rejected.
No evidence family publicly opposed Taliban, West, or Government.
Taliban could hypothetically target anyone in Afghanistan, but no evidence claimants are more likely targets than others.
It is possible the minor could be kidnapped for forced recruitment, but evidence shows only a mere possibility, not a serious one.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds no evidence Taliban targeted the claimants more than other Afghans, and the minor's forced recruitment is only a mere possibility.

propositions.text: The Panel finds the claimants are not Convention refugees under s. 96 of IRPA.
The Panel finds the claimants are not persons in need of protection under s. 97 of IRPA.
The claims are rejected for all claimants for the reasons noted above.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel concludes the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection and rejects their claims.
